soil-water-031.title: Wind abrasion: sandblasting that mattered less than thought
soil-water-031.text: Desert mushroom rocks were once blamed on blowing sand. Wind abrasion, also called corrasion, is the wearing of rock and landforms by wind-driven grains. It was long thought a major cause of desert erosion, but by the mid-20th century it was judged much less important. Mushroom rocks are now credited to other processes. Wind rarely lifts sand far: most stays within 50 cm of the surface, and practically none rises above 2 m. Yardangs, rock ridges up to tens of metres high streamlined by desert winds, are widely attributed to abrasion. Polished or faceted stones called ventifacts are rare, needing abundant sand, strong winds and no vegetation.

soil-water-093.title: Silt fences: cheap, simple and often failing
soil-water-093.text: One of the cheapest sediment barriers on a building site also has a poor field record. A silt fence is a temporary fabric fence that keeps sediment in stormwater runoff out of nearby waters. Geotextile fabric is stretched between stakes along a contour, its lower edge buried in the soil, so runoff pools behind it and sediment settles out. Low cost and simple design make it popular. Field tests show generally poor results, often from bad placement, installation or maintenance. Fine particles soon clog the fabric, and no sediment-retention device filters stormwater for long. Since 1998, static slicing has proved the most effective way to install it.

soil-water-063.title: A warming climate can raise or lower landslide risk
soil-water-063.text: Climate change does not push landslides in one direction. Shifts in temperature, rainfall and {{ref:soil-water-161}} change where, how often and how strongly slides occur. The effects vary so much between areas that they must be studied regionally. Warming can reduce landslides where faster evaporation dries soils and plant growth is stimulated. It increases them through faster snowmelt, rain on snow and glacier retreat. At high elevation, thawing frozen ground loses the cohesion its interstitial ice once gave. More extreme rainfall also focuses infiltration and increases runoff events that may trigger debris flows.

soil-water-058.title: Six ways a slope can fail
soil-water-058.text: Falls, topples, slides, spreads, flows and slope deformation: these six types of movement sort landslides in rock and soil alike. Falls are blocks in free fall. Topples rotate away from a vertical face. Slides move as an intact body over planar or spoon-shaped shear surfaces, the latter called rotational. Spreads crack and extend sideways, flows move fluidised dry or wet material, and slope deformations are slow, distributed movements. David Varnes proposed a tighter scheme in 1978. Cruden and Varnes revised it in 1996, and Hungr, Leroueil and Picarelli revised it most recently in 2014.

soil-water-061.title: Mapping where the next landslide will strike
soil-water-061.text: Landslide hazard mapping rests on one assumption: future slides will happen under the same conditions as past ones. Analysts study the factors behind earlier landslides, usually grouped as geomorphology, geology, land use and land cover, and hydrogeology. Geographic information systems handle the many layered factors. Aerial photos and satellite images taken before and after events record where slides happened and what set them off. A good hazard map shows past events and clearly marks probable future sites, so planners can reduce losses.

soil-water-062.title: Watching slopes move to warn of landslides
soil-water-062.text: Landslide monitoring tracks slope movement to judge danger, issue timely alerts and plan protective measures. From above, InSAR measures displacement precisely over large areas, joined by repeated LiDAR point clouds, optical satellite imagery and drones. On the ground, crews use GPS, surveys of marked targets and ground-based radar. Instruments in the slope itself fill in the rest. Piezometers read pore water pressure, extensometers span cracks, and borehole inclinometers and tiltmeters track the ground's deformation.

soil-water-059.title: Shallow slides and deep-seated slides
soil-water-059.text: The depth of a landslide's sliding surface sorts it into one of two families. Shallow slides run within the soil mantle or weathered bedrock, from a few decimetres to some metres deep. Debris slides and debris flows are usually shallow. They often happen where permeable soil lies over less permeable soil, which traps water, builds pressure and lets the saturated topsoil slide. Deep-seated slides lie well below tree rooting depth, in deep {{ref:soil-form-097}}, weathered rock or bedrock. They often move along faults or bedding planes, leaving concave head scarps and steep toes. Over geological time they shape landscapes and feed sediment that strongly alters stream courses.

soil-water-067.title: Trees on a slope: anchor or burden
soil-water-067.text: The same large trees can steady a slope or help bring it down, depending on where they stand. At the toe of a slope prone to rotational failure, they could raise its factor of safety by 10%. Planted at the top, they could lower it by 10%. The link between slopes and plants runs both ways, shaped by soil type, rainfall regime, plant species, slope aspect and steepness. Plants act in four main ways: wind throw, removal of water, their added mass, called surcharge, and reinforcement by roots. Wind throw topples a tree and exposes its root plate, a risk for single trees more than for sheltered stands. Mass matters only for large trees: one 30–50m tall may load a slope with roughly 100–150 kN/m2. Felling big trees at the toe removes both their drying effect and their load. In clay soils the resulting suction can then draw in water and soften the soil.

soil-water-034.title: Dust storms: when dry ground takes to the sky
soil-water-034.text: Saharan dust storms have increased about 10-fold since the 1950s, stripping topsoil from Niger, Chad, northern Nigeria and Burkina Faso. A dust storm, also called a sandstorm, is a storm in which strong wind blows loose sand and dirt off dry ground. By one definition, it carries enough dust to cut visibility below 1 kilometre. The dust is made in the act. Skipping sand grains strike the ground and break off finer dust, which then travels in suspension, as {{ref:soil-water-032}} describes. Gusts come from thunderstorm outflows or from dry cold fronts, the type common in the years of {{ref:soil-water-075}}. Drought, wind, wildfire and poor farming and grazing all cause dust storms. Heavy plowing in dryland farming and bare ground left without crops are especially risky. The losses are selective. Storms take organic matter and the light, nutrient-rich particles first, and their abrasion damages young crops. Inhaled dust can cause dust pneumonia, and prolonged exposure can cause silicosis. Yet deposited dust can also help. Rainforests of Central and South America gain mineral nutrients from the Sahara, and ancient dust deposits form fertile loess.

soil-water-075.title: The Dust Bowl: when the Great Plains blew away
soil-water-075.text: In May 1934 a two-day storm dropped 12 million pounds (5,400 tonnes) of dust on Chicago. The dust was farm soil, lifted by the wind. The Dust Bowl was a decade of severe dust storms and drought, from 1930 to 1940. It badly damaged the farming and ecology of the High Plains and North American prairies. It hit hardest in western Kansas, the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, southeast Colorado and northeast New Mexico. Its drought and erosion affected 100 million acres (400,000 km2). Nature supplied the drought; people had laid the soil bare. Deep plowing of the virgin prairie had removed the native deep-rooted grasses that held soil and moisture through droughts and high winds. Settlers did not use the dryland farming methods that prevent wind erosion. Cotton farmers left fields bare in winter, when High Plains winds are strongest, and burned the stubble, stripping the soil of organic matter and cover. Then drought came in three waves, in 1934, 1936 and 1939–1940. It dried the {{ref:soil-form-021}} to a powder, and failed crops left plowed fields open to the wind. Black blizzards of dust reached the East Coast. By the end of the 1930s, more than 75% of the topsoil had blown away in many regions. A key legacy was a government with a far larger role in managing land and conserving soil.

soil-water-076.title: How Washington fought the Dust Bowl
soil-water-076.text: By 1938 the conservation effort had cut the amount of blowing soil by 65%. It began in August 1933 with the Soil Erosion Service under the soil scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-019}}. In 1935 it moved to the Department of Agriculture and was renamed; today it is the NRCS. The Civilian Conservation Corps planted over 200 million trees from Canada to Abilene, Texas, to break the wind and hold soil and water. Farmers learned to rotate crops, farm in strips, plow along contours and build level steps into slopes. From 1937 they were paid a dollar an acre to do so.

soil-water-077.title: The Dust Bowl's long shadow on farm values
soil-water-077.text: By 1940, relative to low-erosion counties, farmland value per acre had fallen 28% in high-erosion counties and 17% in medium-erosion ones. In highly eroded areas, less than 25% of the original agricultural losses were ever recovered. Thinner topsoil favoured a shift from wheat to livestock and hay, but farmers were slow to switch, partly because bank failures cut off credit. The economy adjusted mainly by losing people. Population fell in the more eroded counties, both in the 1930s and through the 1950s.

soil-water-096.title: River bank failure: when the bank gives way
soil-water-096.text: Every stream eats at its banks by friction, shearing and solution. River bank failure is the sudden mass wasting of a bank, when gravity on its rock and soil exceeds the cohesive and adhesive forces holding them together. Floods, the corkscrewing helicoidal flow on the outside of bends, and downcutting rills and gullies speed the attack. Extra weight near the edge, saturation from rain, watering of crops or septic systems, groundwater undermining and loss of deep-rooted plants can all set off a collapse. The toe zone, between ordinary and low water level, is most exposed. Cohesive soils fail on rotational or planar surfaces; non-cohesive ones avalanche.

soil-water-094.title: The hole erosion test: drilling a leak to measure it
soil-water-094.text: The hole erosion test measures how well a soil resists erosion, above all for {{ref:soil-water-100}} in embankment dams. A small hole, typically 6 mm, is drilled through a soil sample compacted in a mould. Water forced through erodes and widens the hole while the flow is measured. Plotting erosion rate against hydraulic shear stress gives two values. One is the critical shear stress at which a leak starts to erode. The other is the erodibility, which sets how fast erosion then proceeds. A modified version adds a pitot-static tube to measure total head. It gives much smaller critical shear stresses, closer to the jet erosion test.

soil-water-101.title: Earthflows: slow rivers of saturated clay and silt
soil-water-101.text: An earthflow is a viscous downslope flow of water-saturated, fine-grained material moving under gravity. It sits between downhill creep and the faster {{ref:soil-water-060}}, and solid material rides along on its surface. Clay, fine sand, silt and fine pyroclastic material are prone to it once saturated with enough water. More water means faster flow, so an earthflow may take minutes or years to move. It can cover a few square meters or several hectares. Slopes undercut by rivers or construction, or made of wet clay and silt, are most at risk. Draining slopes is one of the best defences.

soil-water-099.title: Sediment basins: settling ponds for building sites
soil-water-099.text: A sediment basin is a temporary pond on a construction site that captures soil washed off in rain storms. Muddy runoff settles in the pond before the water is discharged, protecting nearby waters. Basins suit sites of 5 acres (20,000 m2) or more. Smaller sites use sediment traps, small embankments along low ground or above storm drain inlets. When earthmoving ends, a basin may be cleaned out and kept as a permanent detention or retention basin for stormwater.

soil-water-098.title: Fiber rolls: straw tubes that catch a slope's soil
soil-water-098.text: A fiber roll is a temporary tube of straw, coconut fibre or similar material laid on construction slopes to control erosion and trap sediment. Crews lay the rolls along contours in shallow trenches 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 cm) deep and stake them down. Steeper slopes get more rows, and one goes at the slope's base. The rolls slow surface runoff without channelling it. Water passes through while sediment stays uphill, and properly installed rolls trap sediment better than straw bales. They do not suit very steep land prone to slides or creep, and poorly staked rolls can be carried off by high flows.

soil-water-060.title: Mudflows: liquefied slopes on the run
soil-water-060.text: A mudflow moves at three to five metres per second. It is a fast-moving flow of debris and soil liquefied by added water, also called a mudslide. Mudflows contain at least 50% silt- and clay-sized material and up to 30% water. Their clay makes them more fluid than debris flows, so they travel farther over gentler slopes. Many begin as slides triggered by heavy rain, snowmelt or groundwater and turn into flows as they take up water. Whether mud starts to flow depends on its grain size, water content and the slope.

soil-water-052.title: Clearing muddy runoff with flocculants
soil-water-052.text: Sediment treatment systems clean muddy construction runoff by adding flocculants, chemicals that make fine particles clump, then filtering or settling the water. Active systems pump the water and dose it with natural polymers, synthetic polymers or inorganic flocculants to cut total suspended solids before discharge. The choice matters. Cationic flocculants such as chitosan can cause hypoxia in fish, so anionic ones are best practice in open systems. Passive systems rely on gravity, with self-dosing gel flocculants, jute filters and settling ponds, and need no power and little skill. Stormwater facilities are usually designed with Stokes' law to remove particles larger than 40 microns.

soil-water-251.title: Saltation: grains that travel in hops
soil-water-251.text: Pebbles in rivers, desert sand, soil blowing off fields and drifting snow all travel in hops. In saltation, wind or water lifts loose grains from a bed and carries them in short hops back to the surface. Slow flows only roll grains along as creep. Above the fluid threshold, drag and lift raise them into roughly ballistic arcs. Landing grains splash others into motion, and in air this bombardment makes most of the dust in dust storms. Particles of about 70 micrometres or less ride the turbulence in suspension instead. Fences with holes slow saltation, piling sand on their lee side.

soil-water-028.title: Healing a gully by taming its water
soil-water-028.text: Gully stabilisation alters the water flowing through a gully so it scours less, sediment builds up and plants return. Drop structures, pipe structures, grass chutes and rock chutes carry water safely down to the gully floor. Sediment settling on flatter stretches lets vegetation re-establish, and damaged areas should be fenced off until restoration is complete. Prevention is easier. Vegetation along drainage lines, evenly spread runoff, high soil organic matter and no over-cultivation keep gullies from forming. Evidence on how well gully controls work is scattered, and terrain, climate and landscape can make them fail.
